The United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Island (UK) contains four jurisdictions: England, Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland. The UK Parliament in Westminster, London retains the exclusive power to pass legislation for all jurisdictions on “reserved matters”-for example, the making of peace or war, defense, international trade, foreign relations and other matters of public concern. Wales, Scotland and Northern Island have their own legislative bodies and may pass laws on issues that are known as “devolved matters.” UK legislation are divided into two main categories: primary and secondary legislation. The laws passed by the legislative bodies of the UK (e.g., Acts of the UK Parliament, Scottish Parliament, Welsh Parliament and Northern Ireland Assembly) are “primary legislation” or “statutes”. Secondary legislation (also known as “subordinate” or “delegated” legislation) are equivalent to administrative regulations in the United States-they are specialized rules and regulations issued by ministers or governmental entities with authority delegated to them by an Act of Parliament.

This database compiles legislation and case law from international and local jurisdictions that recognize rights for non-human entities, including animals, rivers, ecosystems, AI, and machines. It also includes cases in which non-human entities have been granted special legal status, even when full legal rights have not been formally recognized. The database is organized by resource type (legislation and judicial decisions) as well as by jurisdiction (international and local). These categories are further subdivided to facilitate ease of use and navigation. Most resources are presented in their original language, and English translations are provided whenever available. When original legislation, case law, or project documents cannot be obtained, alternative sources-such as press articles-are included to provide relevant context. Although still a work in progress, the database aspires to serve as an expanding resource for legal professionals, scholars, and activists engaged in the emerging field of non-human rights.
